questions.question: How does bubble sort work, and what is its time complexity?
questions.title: Bubble sort passes and complexity
questions.direct_answer: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent values and swaps an out-of-order pair. Each pass moves the largest remaining value to the end; it is O(n²) average and worst case, with an O(n) best case when an early-exit flag is used.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Compare adjacent values.
Swap when the left value is larger.
Each pass fixes one value at the end.
An unchanged pass means the array is sorted.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Bubble sort scans adjacent pairs and swaps them when they are out of order. After one full pass, the largest unsorted value has moved to its final position, so the next pass can stop one position earlier.

For example, `[5, 1, 4, 2]` becomes `[1, 4, 2, 5]` after the first pass. The next passes move `4` and then finish `[1, 2, 4, 5]`. A `swapped` flag can stop the algorithm when a pass makes no changes.

The average and worst-case time is O(n²), while an already sorted array with early exit takes O(n). The usual implementation is in place with O(1) extra space and can be stable when equal values are not swapped. It is useful for teaching, but not normally chosen for large real data.

sections.title: The sorted suffix grows after every pass
sections.content:
The invariant is that the last p positions are correct after p completed passes. Adjacent swaps are enough because an oversized value keeps moving right until no smaller neighbour remains after it.

Early exit improves only inputs that become sorted before all passes. It does not change the quadratic worst case, such as an array arranged in descending order.

questions.question: How does merge sort work in JavaScript?
questions.title: Merge sort by divide, sort, and merge
questions.direct_answer: Merge sort splits the array until each part has at most one value, recursively sorts both halves, and merges them by repeatedly taking the smaller front value. It runs in O(n log n) time and normally uses O(n) extra array space.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Split into two halves.
A size-zero or size-one array is sorted.
Merge two sorted halves linearly.
Time is O(n log n); extra space is O(n).

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm. It splits an array into halves until the pieces contain at most one value, then merges sorted pieces into larger sorted arrays.

For example, `[4, 1, 3, 2]` splits into `[4, 1]` and `[3, 2]`, which become `[1, 4]` and `[2, 3]`. The final merge compares the front values and produces `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.

There are log n split levels and O(n) merge work per level, so time is O(n log n) in best, average, and worst cases. A straightforward JavaScript array version uses O(n) auxiliary storage and can be stable by choosing the left value when keys are equal. It is a strong predictable sort when extra memory is acceptable.

sections.title: Linear merging across logarithmic levels
sections.content:
The merge step needs two pointers because both inputs are already sorted. The smaller front value is the smallest remaining value overall, so it can be appended without looking farther ahead.

Slicing arrays at every recursive call adds allocations beyond the merge buffers. Index ranges and reusable temporary storage can reduce allocation pressure, although the algorithm still needs linear auxiliary space for a normal array merge.

questions.question: How does quicksort work, and when does it reach its worst case?
questions.title: Quicksort partitioning and worst-case shape
questions.direct_answer: Quicksort partitions values around a pivot, then sorts the smaller and larger regions. Balanced partitions give O(n log n) average time; repeatedly choosing an extreme pivot creates O(n²) time and O(n) recursion depth.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Choose a pivot.
Partition smaller and larger values.
Sort the partitions recursively.
Highly unbalanced partitions cause the worst case.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Quicksort chooses a pivot and partitions the remaining values so smaller items are on one side and larger items are on the other. It then applies the same process to those regions until each has at most one value.

For example, using `4` as a pivot for `[6, 2, 4, 1, 5]` can produce `[2, 1]`, `4`, and `[6, 5]`. Sorting the two sides gives `[1, 2, 4, 5, 6]`.

Balanced partitions create about log n levels with O(n) partition work per level, giving O(n log n) average time. If the pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest value, the levels become n deep and time becomes O(n²). Randomized or median-style pivot choices reduce that risk. Typical in-place quicksort is not stable and still uses stack space.

sections.title: Partition balance controls recursion depth
sections.content:
Partitioning places the pivot in, or separates it around, its final ordering region without fully sorting either side. The recursive calls can then ignore comparisons across the partition boundary.

A simple functional JavaScript version that builds `smaller` and `larger` arrays is easy to explain but uses additional memory. In-place partition schemes reduce array allocation but require careful index invariants and duplicate handling.

sections.title: Quicksort partition shapes
sections.content:
| Partition shape | Depth | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Roughly balanced | O(log n) | O(n log n) |
| One side empty repeatedly | O(n) | O(n²) |
| Many equal values with three-way partition | Can stay compact | Handles duplicates efficiently |

questions.question: Why does JavaScript numeric sort need a comparator?
questions.title: Numeric comparison with Array sort
questions.direct_answer: Without a comparator, `Array.prototype.sort()` converts elements to strings and compares their UTF-16 sequences. Use `(a, b) => a - b` for ascending numbers and `(a, b) => b - a` for descending numbers.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Default sort compares string forms.
`a - b` sorts numbers ascending.
`b - a` sorts numbers descending.
Modern sort is stable, but it mutates the array.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
JavaScript's default array sort does not perform numeric comparison. It converts elements to strings and orders those strings by UTF-16 code units, so numeric values can appear in an unexpected order.

For example, `[1, 30, 4, 21, 100000].sort()` places `100000` near `1` because its string begins with `'1'`. Calling `.sort((a, b) => a - b)` returns ascending numeric order because a negative result means a comes first and a positive result means b comes first.

`sort()` mutates the original array, so use `toSorted()` or sort a copy when the source must remain unchanged. Current ECMAScript requires stable sorting, meaning items that compare as equal keep their earlier relative order. A comparator must be consistent; returning only a boolean does not satisfy its negative-zero-positive contract.

sections.title: The comparator defines ordering, not filtering
sections.content:
A comparator answers the relative order for a pair: less than zero, zero, or greater than zero. The engine controls which pairs are requested, so the function must be pure and obey a consistent ordering relation.

Subtraction works for ordinary finite numbers. Data containing `NaN`, mixed types, or values requiring locale-aware text order needs an explicit policy rather than assuming the short numeric comparator covers every case.

questions.question: How do you choose a sorting algorithm in an interview?
questions.title: Sorting choice from constraints
questions.direct_answer: Choose from the input size, existing order, memory limit, stability requirement, key range, and whether mutation is allowed. State the standard library sort first when permitted, then explain when a specialized algorithm changes the trade-off.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Read size and value constraints first.
Ask whether equal-key order must remain stable.
Include extra space and mutation in the choice.
A bounded integer range may allow counting sort.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A sorting choice begins with the contract rather than a favourite algorithm. Important facts are n, how ordered the input already is, whether equal items must keep their order, available memory, mutation rules, and the type or range of keys.

For example, general user records can use the language's stable O(n log n)-class built-in sort with a clear comparator. Millions of small non-negative integers in a narrow known range may suit counting sort. A linked list can suit merge sort because merging does not require random array access.

Quicksort offers strong average performance and in-place partitioning but has an O(n²) worst case without safeguards and is usually unstable. Merge sort has predictable O(n log n) time and stability but needs extra merge storage for arrays. In an interview, name the chosen properties and complexity, then mention the closest rejected alternative and why the constraints favour the choice.

sections.title: Sorting constraints form a decision table
sections.content:
Comparison sorts have an Ω(n log n) lower bound in the general comparison model. Counting and radix-style methods can do better only by using stronger information about the keys, such as a bounded integer range or fixed digit representation.

The platform sort is normally the production default because it is tested and optimized. Implementing a named algorithm is appropriate when the question asks for it or when a property such as stable external merging or bounded-key counting is central to the problem.

sections.title: Common sorting trade-offs
sections.content:
| Algorithm | Typical time | Extra space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Built-in numeric sort | Implementation-guaranteed ordering behavior | Engine dependent | Yes |
| Merge sort | O(n log n) | O(n) for arrays | Yes |
| Quicksort | O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst | Stack plus partition | Usually no |
| Counting sort | O(n + range) | O(range) | Can be |
